title: Great Onboarding Makes People Feel as if They Belong Right Away
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: The move here is a careful distinction between belonging and three softer states most onboarding programs aim for: fitting in, feeling welcome, and being accepted. Those are all passive states, conferred on the newcomer by the existing team. Belonging is different. Belonging is being treated as an insider from day one: remembered, included, taken seriously, free to speak candidly without fear of rejection, and able to influence decisions. The new hire stops performing to fit in and shows up authentically because they are considered a permanent part of the place. The authors note that most organizations are reasonably good at welcoming and accepting newcomers but rarely work to produce this deeper sense of belonging from the outset. Research, they note, is clear that the sooner people feel they belong, the faster they engage, the more likely they are to stay, and the closer they come to their highest potential. Great organizations therefore engineer instant belonging deliberately rather than hoping it emerges. Three concrete best practices anchor the piece. Give new team members autonomy over the onboarding process itself by offering a menu of activities and letting them choose the order, which signals that they already have influence. Pair new hires with other recent hires so integration stories can be exchanged, which supplies the validation belonging requires. And assign a low-risk decision or small improvement early, because real belonging means the newcomer can shape the system rather than just absorb it. For a school leader onboarding a new teacher or TA, the translation is straightforward: offer a choice of induction paths, pair them with someone who joined last year, and give them a small, real decision to own within the first two weeks.
points: Belonging (being treated as an insider with genuine influence) is fundamentally different from fitting in, feeling welcome, or being accepted, yet most onboarding targets the passive states instead.

The sooner new team members feel they belong, the faster they engage, the more likely they stay, and the closer they come to their highest potential,belonging is a business imperative, not just culture.

Giving new hires a menu of onboarding activities to self-direct signals instant influence; pairing them with recent hires provides validation; assigning a real (low-risk) decision demonstrates they can shape the system.
When newcomers are asked to perform to fit in rather than show up authentically, they withhold exactly the independent thinking and voice that real belonging requires.
quotes: For newcomers, belonging is an entirely different experience from fitting in, feeling welcome, or being accepted. Belonging means the new team member is treated as an “insider” and they can be themselves by speaking candidly without the fear of rejection.

When new team members belong, they feel valued as a person, not just for the role they play or the skills they possess. Those who truly belong are remembered, included, and taken seriously. Their voice carries weight and can influence decisions.

As a rule, organizations are certainly apt to welcome or accept newcomers, but seldom work hard to make them feel that they are an integral part of the team from the get-go. Research shows that the sooner people feel they belong, the more likely they are to engage fully, commit to staying, and perform to their highest potential.

Instead of a highly structured process of acclimation, good organizations give new hires a menu of onboarding activities and let them choose what to prioritize (shadowing, process, product or service deep dives, organizational history, customer or client calls). By making the onboarding process somewhat self-directed, the organization signals that the new team member has instant influence over how things happen.

Belonging requires validation, so another best practice is to pair up new team members with other recent hires so they can share their integration stories. When newcomers learn how quickly others become an integral part of the organization, it bolsters their own sense of inclusion and attachment.

Lastly, leaders who want to create a sense of belonging with new hires assign them to a low-risk decision or improvement to show that they can shape the system. Those who truly belong can have immediate influence over others. This assignment demonstrates that.

Even in the workplace, people search for a place they can call home. When they find it, the organization benefits from a newfound loyalty and commitment. It’s up to leaders to create it. When team members are treated like they belong, then they do.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
